rows.fidelity_note: The paper introduces token streams and whitespace; the formal definition also requires explicit token delimiters and permits a final comment without a line break. These are additional parsing conventions, so this is not a literal transcription of the quoted rules.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.From
rows.annotation: The token stream in this passage is the output of the relation in `Tokenization.From`. A step splits off whitespace and one token, records its byte offset, leaves the token's source spelling intact, and continues on the rest. The rules require a delimiter after a non-parenthesis token and admit a final comment at end of input.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition recognizes a semicolon followed by characters up to and including the first line feed or carriage return. This completes the comment rule whose sentence continues onto the next page.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.comment
rows.plain: Semicolon comments stop at the first line break
rows.annotation: In `|a;b|`, the semicolon is part of the quoted name. A semicolon at a token boundary starts a comment, and the `comment` expression consumes through the first line feed or carriage return. The tokenization rules determine which situation applies.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper speaks of Unicode characters from 128 onward; the formal definition recognizes individual bytes from 32 to 126 or 128 to 255. This models an encoded byte stream and does not validate its Unicode encoding.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.printableChar
rows.annotation: The printable character class in this paragraph corresponds to two byte ranges in Lean, $32$ through $126$ and $128$ through $255$. A UTF-8 character can span several bytes, and this regular expression matches one byte at a time.

ties.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization
ties.plain: Splitting input into lexical tokens

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition starts tokenization at offset zero, treats whitespace as separators, and adds a delimiter requirement after non-parenthesis tokens. It also allows an unterminated final comment; the quotation does not specify these extra conventions.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization
rows.annotation: In `(assert x)`, the tokens start at byte offsets 0, 1, 8 and 9. The space after `assert` is consumed, leaving a gap in the offsets. `Tokenization` starts the `From` relation at offset zero, so the parser receives tokens that still point to their positions in the original input.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition tracks token positions while discarding separating whitespace. It additionally requires delimiters after non-parenthesis tokens and allows a comment to end at end of input, neither of which is stated in the quotation.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.From
rows.annotation: Try splitting `1.5` after `1`. The next byte `.` is outside the allowed delimiters, so that split cannot be a `From.token` step. Taking `1.5` together as a decimal works. This is how the formal delimitation rule keeps one literal from turning into two tokens.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition assigns recognition rules to parentheses, numeric literals, strings, symbols, keywords, and reserved words. Simple and quoted symbols are represented separately; the keyword rule has the broader spelling discussed at the keyword passage.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.categoryRegex
rows.plain: Regular expressions for token categories by version
rows.annotation: The standard's list of token kinds becomes a case split in `categoryRegex`, with separate cases for simple and quoted symbols. The selected version determines the reserved words and simple-symbol rule, and version 2.0 uses its own string rule.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition ends a semicolon comment at the first line feed or carriage return, matching the sentence continued here. Recognition of comments within the source is handled separately from recognition of string literals and quoted symbols.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.comment
rows.plain: Semicolon comments stop at the first line break
rows.annotation: The regex separates an ordinary comment into three pieces. `lit ";"` starts it, `star (minus anyChar lineBreak)` accepts its body, and `lineBreak` consumes the first following line feed or carriage return. Thus when a line starts with `; note`, the line break is consumed with that comment and the text on the next line remains for tokenization. A final comment without a line break is handled by the separate `commentAtEnd` rule.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition allows exactly character codes 10 and 13 as comment-ending line breaks, as stated in the paper.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.lineBreak
rows.annotation: `alt (code 10) (code 13)` matches one byte, a line feed or a carriage return. That byte ends the ordinary semicolon comment.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition recognizes any concatenation of whitespace characters and line-terminated comments, including an empty concatenation. This supplies the separators described in the paper.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.whitespace
rows.annotation: In `star (alt whiteSpaceChar comment)`, each repetition consumes either a white space byte or a complete line-terminated comment. Zero repetitions allow an empty separator, and the tokenization relation specifies when a delimiter is required.

rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.whiteSpaceChar
rows.plain: Tab, line feed, carriage return and space
rows.annotation: The four alternatives in `altAll` are the decimal byte codes for tab, line feed, carriage return and space. A sequence of such bytes is handled by the separate `whitespace` expression.

rows.plain: Decimal literals have digits on both sides of the point
rows.annotation: The two occurrences of `numeral` enclose a literal point followed by `star (lit "0")`. The extra zero run makes `0.007` possible on the fractional side, and the final numeral ensures at least one digit follows the point.

ties.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.hexadecimal

rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.hexadecimal
rows.plain: Hexadecimal literals have a #x prefix and a nonempty digit string
rows.annotation: The literal prefix is `#x`. The following `plus` requires at least one byte from the digit class or the two letter ranges `A` to `F` and `a` to `f`, as in `#x01Ab`.

ties.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.binary
ties.plain: Binary literals have a #b prefix and a nonempty digit string

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition requires the lowercase prefix #b followed by one or more characters, each either 0 or 1.
rows.name: BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.binary
rows.plain: Binary literals have a #b prefix and a nonempty digit string
rows.annotation: For the standard's `#b001`, `seq` joins the fixed prefix `#b` to three individual matches of `oneOf "01"`. The `plus` combinator means one or more repetitions, so `#b` alone fails.
